**Text 1**

The following text is from Frederick Douglass's 1845 autobiography *Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass, an American Slave*. Douglass's enslaver, Mr. Auld, has just forbidden his wife to keep teaching the young Douglass to read.

The very decided manner with which he spoke, and strove to impress his wife with the evil consequences of giving me instruction, served to convince me that he was deeply sensible of the truths he was uttering. … What he most dreaded, that I most desired. What he most loved, that I most hated. That which to him was a great evil, to be carefully shunned, was to me a great good, to be diligently sought; and the argument which he so warmly urged, against my learning to read, only served to inspire me with a desire and determination to learn.

**Text 2**

In the decades before the Civil War, several Southern states passed laws making it a crime to teach enslaved people to read or write. Historian Malika Yusupova argues that these laws reveal what enslavers themselves believed: that literacy would allow enslaved people to read antislavery writings, forge travel passes, and communicate with one another, making slavery harder to maintain.
stem: Based on the texts, how would Yusupova (Text 2) most likely view Mr. Auld's attitude as Douglass describes it in Text 1?
option_a: As an unusual opinion that few other enslavers shared
option_b: As typical of a widespread belief among enslavers that literacy threatened slavery
option_c: As evidence that enslavers secretly wanted enslaved people to learn to read
option_d: As proof that laws against teaching enslaved people to read were rarely passed
explanation_en:
Mr. Auld fears the “evil consequences” of teaching Douglass to read. Yusupova argues that laws in several states show enslavers generally believed literacy would make slavery “harder to maintain.” She would therefore see Mr. Auld's attitude as typical of that belief, as choice B says.

Choice A is wrong because Yusupova describes this belief as widespread enough to produce laws in several states. Choice C contradicts both texts: Mr. Auld forbids reading lessons, and Text 2 describes laws banning them. Choice D contradicts Text 2, which says several states passed such laws.

For much of the twentieth century, textbooks and magazines often repeated the claim that the Great Wall of China is the only human-made structure that can be seen with the naked eye from space. The claim appeared in print decades before anyone had actually traveled into orbit.

**Text 2**

Astronauts orbiting Earth at about 400 kilometers have generally reported that they could not pick out the Great Wall without a camera lens. Although the wall is very long, it is only a few meters wide, and it is built of materials similar in color to the land around it. stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim described in Text 1?

option_c: By arguing that the claim is true only at night, when the wall is lit
option_d: By suggesting that the claim was based on careful observations made from orbit
explanation_en:
Text 1's claim has two parts: the wall can be seen with the naked eye from space, and it is the only human-made structure that can. Text 2 contradicts both parts: astronauts generally could not see the wall without a lens, and they easily see airports and lit cities. The author would reject the claim, as choice A says.

Choice B is wrong because Text 2 says the wall is hard to see despite its length, because it is narrow and similar in color to its surroundings. Choice C is wrong because Text 2 mentions lit cities, not a lit wall. Choice D is wrong because Text 1 says the claim appeared “decades before anyone had actually traveled into orbit,” so it could not have come from observations made there.

Some educators argue that schools should stop teaching handwriting. Since students now do most of their writing on keyboards, they say, the hours spent practicing letters by hand would be better used for other subjects.

**Text 2**

Educational psychologist Zuhra Olimova asked two groups of university students to take notes on the same lecture, one group by hand and the other on laptops. option_d: She would argue that handwriting is useful only for students who type slowly.
explanation_en:
The educators in Text 1 claim handwriting practice is no longer worth the time. Olimova found that students who took notes by hand remembered main concepts better, possibly because writing by hand makes them summarize. She would therefore warn that handwriting may still have learning benefits, as choice C says.

Choice A contradicts her results: the handwriting group did better. Choice B is wrong because her study gives her a reason to question, not support, the educators' view, and she says nothing about how often students write by hand. **Text 1**

The following text is from the opening of Henry David Thoreau's 1862 essay “Walking.”

I wish to speak a word for Nature, for absolute Freedom and Wildness, as contrasted with a freedom and culture merely civil,—to regard man as an inhabitant, or a part and parcel of Nature, rather than a member of society. I wish to make an extreme statement, if so I may make an emphatic one, for there are enough champions of civilization: the minister and the school committee and every one of you will take care of that.

**Text 2**

Urban ecologist Kamola Nurmatova studies the foxes, hawks, and wildflowers that thrive in the parks, rail yards, and empty lots of large cities. She argues that treating “nature” and “civilization” as opposites has led people to overlook the wildlife all around them. In her view, a city is not the absence of nature but one of the places where nature now exists, and protecting urban habitats deserves as much attention as protecting remote wilderness.
stem: Based on the texts, how would Nurmatova (Text 2) most likely respond to the way Thoreau frames his discussion in Text 1?
option_a: She would agree that champions of civilization have ignored wild places far from cities.
option_b: She would argue that people should be regarded as members of society rather than as part of Nature.
option_c: She would claim that Thoreau's statement is not extreme enough.
option_d: She would question his contrast between Nature and civilized society, since she sees cities themselves as places where nature exists.
explanation_en:
Thoreau frames his essay as speaking for Nature “as contrasted with” civil society and civilization. Nurmatova argues that treating nature and civilization “as opposites” causes people to miss the wildlife in cities, which she sees as places “where nature now exists.” She would therefore question the contrast Thoreau draws, as choice D says.

Choice A is wrong because Nurmatova's concern is that people overlook nature inside cities, not wild places far from them. Choice B is wrong because nothing in Text 2 suggests she would separate people from nature; her view blurs that line. Choice C is wrong because Text 2 gives no reason to think she wants Thoreau's opposition between nature and civilization made even sharper.

Drays, carts, men, boys, all go hurrying from many quarters to a common center, the wharf. Assembled there, the people fasten their eyes upon the coming boat as upon a wonder they are seeing for the first time. Historian Rustam Karimov notes that in the mid-1800s, steamboat companies competed fiercely for passengers and freight in the towns along the Mississippi. option_d: As evidence that steamboat companies did not compete with one another
explanation_en:

He would see the smoke as a deliberate show for potential customers, as choice A says.

Choice B is wrong because both texts present the smoke as intentional, not accidental. Choice C is wrong because neither text links the smoke to engine trouble. Choice D contradicts Text 2, which says the companies “competed fiercely.”

**Text 1**

The following text is from the Introduction to the 1872 edition of Charles Darwin's *On the Origin of Species*.

Although much remains obscure, and will long remain obscure, I can entertain no doubt, after the most deliberate study and dispassionate judgment of which I am capable, that the view which most naturalists until recently entertained, and which I formerly entertained—namely, that each species has been independently created—is erroneous. I am fully convinced that species are not immutable; but that those belonging to what are called the same genera are lineal descendants of some other and generally extinct species … Furthermore, I am convinced that natural selection has been the most important, but not the exclusive, means of modification.

**Text 2**

Biologists today recognize several processes besides natural selection that change populations over time. One of the most studied is genetic drift: random changes in how common a gene variant is, which occur simply because some individuals happen to leave more offspring than others for reasons unrelated to their traits. In very small populations, drift can cause a variant to spread or disappear entirely, regardless of whether it helps or harms the organisms that carry it.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Darwin's final claim in Text 1?
option_a: By rejecting it, since modern biologists have shown that natural selection plays no role in changing populations
option_b: By arguing that Darwin underestimated how strongly natural selection controls small populations
option_c: By claiming that genetic drift shows that species are immutable after all
option_d: By noting that genetic drift is consistent with Darwin's view that natural selection is not the only means of modification
explanation_en:
Darwin's final claim is that natural selection is “the most important, but not the exclusive, means of modification.” Text 2 describes genetic drift as one of “several processes besides natural selection that change populations.” The author of Text 2 would see drift as an example of the kind of non-selective change Darwin allowed for, as choice D says.

Choice A is wrong because Text 2 says other processes exist “besides natural selection,” which implies that selection still operates. Choice B is wrong because Text 2 says that in small populations drift can override whether a variant “helps or harms” its carriers, which suggests selection is weaker there, not stronger. Choice C is wrong because drift is described as a process that changes populations, which supports Darwin's view that species are not immutable.

The following text is from W. E. B. Du Bois's 1903 book *The Souls of Black Folk*. Du Bois has been describing the “double-consciousness” of Black Americans, who feel torn between two identities.

The history of the American Negro is the history of this strife,—this longing to attain self-conscious manhood, to merge his double self into a better and truer self. In this merging he wishes neither of the older selves to be lost. He would not Africanize America, for America has too much to teach the world and Africa. He would not bleach his Negro soul in a flood of white Americanism, for he knows that Negro blood has a message for the world. He simply wishes to make it possible for a man to be both a Negro and an American, without being cursed and spit upon by his fellows, without having the doors of Opportunity closed roughly in his face.

**Text 2**

Psychologists who study people with two cultural backgrounds describe several ways of handling such identities. Some people give up one identity in favor of the other; some keep the two strictly separate, behaving one way at home and another in public. Others, whom researchers call “integrated,” come to see their two identities as compatible parts of a single self. Studies suggest, however, that reaching this integration depends heavily on whether the surrounding society treats both identities with respect.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the researchers described in Text 2 most likely characterize the goal Du Bois describes in Text 1?
option_a: As an example of giving up one identity in favor of the other
option_b: As a form of integration whose achievement would depend on the kind of respectful treatment that Du Bois says is being denied
option_c: As a strategy of keeping two identities strictly separate in different settings
option_d: As a goal that no person with two cultural backgrounds could ever reach
explanation_en:
Du Bois describes a wish “to merge his double self into a better and truer self” while losing neither identity—to be “both a Negro and an American.” This matches what Text 2 calls integration: seeing two identities “as compatible parts of a single self.” Text 2 adds that integration depends on society respecting both identities, and Du Bois says this goal requires not being “cursed and spit upon” or having doors “closed roughly in his face.” Choice B captures both connections.

Choice A is wrong because Du Bois explicitly rejects giving up either identity (“neither of the older selves to be lost”). Choice C is wrong because Du Bois wants to merge the two selves, not keep them apart. Choice D is wrong because Text 2 describes integration as something people do reach under the right conditions.
